paragraphs: Data-driven algorithm design chooses an algorithm’s tunable parameters using examples of the problems it will solve. The computational challenge is finding settings that minimize the loss across those examples, a task called empirical risk minimization. This paper studies how to make that search efficient for combinatorial algorithms with several parameters.

For a fixed problem instance, changing parameters often produces regions where the loss behaves regularly, separated by sharp transitions. The authors enumerate the regions of the combined loss across training instances. Their method is output-sensitive: its running time scales with how many regions actually occur, rather than a worst-case bound on how many could occur.

Two constructions support this approach. A computational geometry algorithm enumerates regions formed by hyperplanes, while an execution graph compactly represents algorithm states reachable under different parameter settings. The paper develops applications to pricing, linkage-based clustering, and sequence alignment using dynamic programming. The contribution connects parameter-search cost to the structure present in the training problems.
neurips-2024-accelerating-erm-for-data-d.tldr: An output-sensitive approach accelerates algorithm parameter learning by making search cost depend on the loss regions that actually occur.

paragraphs: Pairwise comparisons can make subjective judgments easier: an annotator compares two items instead of assigning each an absolute score. Comparing every pair quickly becomes impractical, so a learning system must decide which comparisons are most useful. This paper studies that choice while using item attributes to learn rankings that also extend to unseen items.

The authors derive an upper bound on the expected ordering error of a logistic preference model, expressed in terms of the comparisons collected. They then choose comparisons to reduce this bound. The strategy accounts for both uncertainty arising from noisy judgments and uncertainty arising from incomplete model knowledge. This matters because variation in comparison noise can itself reveal similarity between items.

The study evaluates the algorithm and a variant intended to reduce model misspecification on realistic ranking tasks with human comparisons. The reported results show better annotation efficiency and generalization than non-contextual ranking methods and active preference learning baselines. The findings support using shared item structure and both kinds of uncertainty together when deciding what to ask annotators.
neurips-2024-active-preference-learning-.tldr: A comparison-selection strategy uses item attributes and two kinds of uncertainty to learn rankings more efficiently and generalize to new items.

paragraphs: Adam is widely used to train neural networks, but its theoretical convergence depends on choosing its second-moment hyperparameter, beta_2, in a way that suits the problem. Earlier attempts to repair this issue can require a uniform bound on gradient noise. This paper introduces ADOPT to remove these particular obstacles to a convergence guarantee.

ADOPT makes two changes to the update calculation. It excludes the current gradient from the second-moment estimate used for normalization, and it changes the order of normalization and the momentum update. These modifications alter how gradient information enters the adaptive update. The authors prove an optimal convergence rate of O(1/√T), for any choice of beta_2, without requiring uniformly bounded gradient noise.

The paper also tests ADOPT on image classification, generative modeling, natural language processing, and deep reinforcement learning. It reports better results than Adam and its variants across the evaluated tasks. The contribution combines a stronger convergence result with empirical evidence that the modified update can be useful in varied deep learning settings.
neurips-2024-adopt-modified-adam-can-con.tldr: ADOPT modifies Adam’s update to obtain an optimal convergence rate for any beta_2 without assuming uniformly bounded gradient noise.

paragraphs: Evaluating uncertainty in image segmentation requires images that are challenging and whose uncertainty can be controlled. Simple synthetic examples offer control but little complexity, while real images make the underlying uncertainty difficult to disentangle. Arctique addresses this gap with procedurally generated images modeled on colon histopathology, where intricate structures and variable appearances create demanding segmentation problems.

The authors build a Blender-based system that creates three-dimensional scenes and renders them into images. The dataset contains up to 50,000 images, precise segmentation masks, and simulations of noisy labels. Crucially, the system can adjust uncertainty in the images separately from uncertainty in their labels, giving researchers distinct controls over these sources of difficulty.

The paper demonstrates how these controls support studying several commonly used uncertainty quantification methods. Its contribution is a benchmark environment that combines visual complexity with deliberate experimental manipulation. Public code allows researchers to recreate supplied images, modify them under controlled conditions, and generate new scenes for further evaluation.
neurips-2024-arctique-an-artificial-hist.tldr: Arctique provides complex synthetic tissue images with independently controllable image and label uncertainty for evaluating segmentation uncertainty methods.

paragraphs: Digital twins simulate how real systems change over time, supporting prediction and decision-making. A central challenge is generalizing to unfamiliar conditions when little data is available. This paper examines hybrid digital twins, which combine mechanistic components reflecting domain knowledge with neural components that provide flexible modeling capacity. Their modular structure also supports later changes to the model.

Existing hybrid approaches commonly depend on experts to specify the architecture before fitting its parameters. HDTwinGen instead uses an evolutionary process in which language models propose model specifications. Offline tools optimize the proposed parameters, and evaluations provide targeted feedback. The system uses that feedback to revise and evolve its candidate hybrid models.

The reported experiments show that HDTwinGen produces models with useful generalization, sample efficiency, and capacity for modification. The approach makes architecture design part of the automated learning process alongside parameter fitting. Its significance is the ability to search for combinations of partial domain knowledge and neural modeling, rather than requiring an expert to choose that combination in advance.
neurips-2024-automatically-learning-hybr.tldr: HDTwinGen uses language models and evolutionary feedback to automatically design hybrid simulations combining domain knowledge with neural components.

paragraphs: Prediction intervals express uncertainty by returning a range of possible outcomes. Their usefulness depends on properties such as their width and how coverage behaves under different conditions. This paper introduces a procedure for adapting conformal prediction intervals toward selected goals, including shorter intervals or closer agreement with a target level of conditional coverage.

The method starts with an existing conformity score, the scoring function used to construct conformal intervals. It then applies machine learning techniques, particularly gradient boosting, to improve that function. Carefully designed losses measure how far the resulting intervals deviate from the desired properties, giving the improvement process a specific objective.

The procedure runs after the predictive model has been trained and uses its predictions without changing the model itself. Experiments starting from conventional conformal methods report substantial reductions in interval length and in deviation from target conditional coverage. These findings support adjusting the uncertainty procedure as a practical way to improve interval behavior around an already trained predictor; they do not assert exact conditional coverage.
neurips-2024-boosted-conformal-predictio.tldr: Gradient boosting refines conformal scoring functions after model training to produce shorter intervals or improve alignment with target conditional coverage.

paragraphs: Human smell perception is difficult to study with machine learning partly because large datasets linking molecules to human odor judgments are scarce. This paper asks whether transformers pretrained on general chemical structures already encode information that corresponds to how people perceive smells. The question concerns the alignment of learned molecular representations with human judgments.

The authors examine that alignment across multiple datasets and three forms of perceptual evidence. They test whether the representations predict expert-assigned odor labels, people’s numerical ratings for predefined odor descriptors, and human judgments of similarity between odorants. Together, these tests examine both descriptions of individual odors and perceived relationships between different odors.

The reported results show strong alignment between the pretrained representations and human olfactory perception. The authors also investigate how much of this alignment is associated with physicochemical features known to matter for odor decoding. The findings indicate that general chemical pretraining can provide representations useful for predicting several kinds of human smell judgments, despite the limited availability of large perception-labeled datasets.
neurips-2024-can-transformers-smell-like.tldr: Transformers pretrained on chemical structures learn representations that strongly align with several kinds of human odor judgments.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a language model by training a small portion of its parameters. CorDA addresses the problem that adapters are often constructed without considering either the target task or knowledge worth preserving. It uses representative examples to orient a decomposition of the model’s weights before selecting components to train.

For each linear layer, CorDA combines its weights with an input-activation covariance matrix and performs singular value decomposition. Applying the inverse covariance matrix to the components reconstructs the original weights. In knowledge-preserved adaptation, question-answering examples guide this process, and the components with the smallest singular values initialize the trainable adapter. In instruction-previewed adaptation, task instructions guide the decomposition, and the largest components are trained.

Experiments cover mathematics, coding, and instruction following. The knowledge-preserved version improves task performance over LoRA while reducing forgetting of world knowledge. The instruction-previewed version further improves task performance, reaching results comparable to full fine-tuning and surpassing the named parameter-efficient alternatives. The findings show how representative context can guide which parts of a model are adapted.
neurips-2024-corda-context-oriented-deco.tldr: CorDA uses representative data to construct task-aware adapters that can prioritize preserving knowledge or improving performance on a new task.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning agents make decisions by treating experience and actions as sequences. Transformers can use task context, including multiple trajectories, to improve behavior during online interaction. However, attention becomes computationally expensive as that context grows. This paper explores Mamba as a way to support decisions that depend on long histories.

The authors first create Decision Mamba by replacing the backbone of Decision Transformer. They then introduce a hybrid architecture, DM-H, that assigns complementary roles to Mamba and a transformer. Mamba extracts high-value sub-goals from long-term memory. Those sub-goals become prompts for the transformer, which uses them to produce high-quality predictions.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on both long- and short-term tasks, including D4RL, Grid World, and Tmaze benchmarks. In the reported long-term task, online testing is 28 times faster than transformer-based baselines. The findings support using an efficient sequence model to summarize long experience into sub-goals that guide a transformer, with the speed result tied to the evaluated setting.
neurips-2024-decision-mamba-reinforcemen.tldr: Decision Mamba-Hybrid uses Mamba-generated sub-goals to guide a transformer, improving tested decision tasks while accelerating long-term online evaluation.

paragraphs: Large language models can be difficult to deploy on devices with limited memory and computation. Structural pruning reduces these costs by removing model structures. Existing approaches face a design constraint: they either preserve dependencies between structures, restricting what can be removed, or add projection matrices that introduce additional parameters.

DISP-LLM relaxes the dependence between structures along the embedding dimension. This allows different blocks to retain different subsets of feature maps. It also lets blocks have different widths at their inputs and outputs. The central contribution is greater freedom to choose which structures each block needs, rather than enforcing the same structural choices across dependent parts of the model.

The authors evaluate the method on OPT, LLaMA, LLaMA-2, Phi-1.5, and Phi-2. They report better results than other state-of-the-art approaches and accuracy similar to semi-structural pruning. These experiments indicate that structural pruning can retain competitive accuracy when its design space is made more flexible, strengthening its potential for reducing the resource demands of language models.
neurips-2024-disp-llm-dimension-independ.tldr: DISP-LLM makes structural pruning more flexible by letting language-model blocks retain different features and use different input and output widths.

paragraphs: This paper studies how information pathways through attention heads contribute to prediction and generalization. The authors analyze a deep multi-head self-attention network closely related to transformers but mathematically tractable. Their statistical mechanics theory describes Bayesian learning when network width and the number of training examples both grow while their ratio remains of constant order.

Within that limit, the authors derive exact equations for predictor statistics. These statistics combine kernels associated with pairs of attention paths, where a path passes through particular heads across layers. A task-dependent weighting mechanism aligns the combined kernel with the training labels. The theory identifies this interaction between paths as a source of improved generalization.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world sequence classification support the theoretical findings. The analysis also connects kernel weighting to properties of learned network weights, allowing qualitative insights to carry over to gradient-descent training. As an application, the authors prune attention heads judged less relevant by the theory and demonstrate efficient network size reduction. The exact results concern the specified model and limit.
neurips-2024-dissecting-the-interplay-of.tldr: A tractable attention-network theory explains how task-dependent interactions between attention paths improve generalization and guide head pruning.

paragraphs: Visual experience changes continuously, but much previous brain-decoding research has focused on static images. EEG2Video investigates reconstructing dynamic visual stimuli from electroencephalography. EEG records brain activity at high temporal resolution, here described as 1000 Hz, making it relevant to studying the rapid changes involved in watching moving scenes.

The authors collect paired EEG and video data from 20 participants watching 1,400 clips spanning 40 concepts. They also annotate the clips with information such as color, motion, and whether humans appear. These annotations support investigating which properties of a viewed video can be decoded from the associated brain signals.

Their reconstruction baseline uses a sequence-to-sequence architecture to better align visual motion with temporally detailed EEG recordings. It achieves 79.8% accuracy on a two-way semantic classification task and a structural similarity score of 0.256. These results provide evidence for progress in decoding dynamic perception, while the dataset establishes paired observations for further research. The contribution combines a new experimental resource with a model designed around the temporal nature of the signals.
neurips-2024-eeg2video-towards-decoding-.tldr: EEG2Video introduces paired brain-signal and video data plus a sequence model for reconstructing dynamic visual perception from EEG.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate the factors that explain complex data. Many numerical measures have been proposed to assess this separation, but the properties represented by those scores can be unclear. This paper develops a principled connection between logical definitions of disentanglement and quantitative measures derived from those definitions.

The approach converts a higher-order logical statement into a real-valued quantity through a sequence of substitutions. Equality becomes a strict premetric, binary truth-value algebra becomes an algebra of continuous values called a quantale, and quantifiers become aggregation operations. This compositional process gives the resulting score a mathematical relationship to the property expressed by the original logical statement.

The derived metrics have theoretical guarantees, and some are differentiable enough to serve directly as training objectives. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that the metrics can isolate different aspects of disentangled representations. The contribution therefore concerns both evaluation and learning: it provides a way to make the meaning of a score more explicit and, in some cases, optimize that meaning during training.
neurips-2024-enriching-disentanglement-f.tldr: A compositional mathematical framework turns logical definitions of disentanglement into interpretable numerical metrics, some usable as training objectives.

paragraphs: Observing how cells or animals move together does not directly reveal the interaction rules producing that motion. This paper develops a framework for estimating equations of motion from recorded trajectories. It focuses on interactions between pairs of agents, including non-reciprocal interactions, where the influence of one agent on another need not be matched in reverse.

The framework combines graph neural networks with neural differential equations. Together, these components model pairwise interactions from the states of the interacting entities and connect those interactions to motion over time. The objective is to recover the functional forms of the interaction rules, giving an account of how individual responses produce collective movement.

The authors conduct two numerical experiments. They first tune hyperparameters using a simulated toy system, then apply those settings to a more complex model whose non-reciprocal forces mimic slime-mold cell dynamics. The reported results accurately recover interaction functions and reproduce individual and collective behavior in those systems. The evidence therefore demonstrates recovery of asymmetric interaction rules in the evaluated simulations.
neurips-2024-integrating-gnn-and-neural-.tldr: A graph-network and neural-differential-equation framework recovers pairwise interaction rules, including asymmetric forces, from simulated collective-motion trajectories.

paragraphs: Language models can help robots interpret instructions and plan high-level actions, but confident mistakes can produce unsafe behavior or plans that miss the user’s goal. Instructions can also be genuinely ambiguous. Introspective planning aims to make a planner’s uncertainty better reflect that ambiguity, improving its decisions about both action and clarification.

The method builds a knowledge base of reasoning examples associated with safe, compliant plans selected by humans. These explanations are constructed after the plans are chosen and retrieved during deployment. They guide the language model in refining its own reasoning and uncertainty using examples grounded in human judgments about appropriate plans.

Evaluations on three tasks, including a new safe mobile manipulation benchmark, show substantial improvements in safety and compliance over state-of-the-art language-model planning approaches. When combined with conformal prediction, introspective planning empirically yields tighter confidence bounds while maintaining statistical success guarantees and reducing unnecessary clarification requests. The findings connect improved uncertainty handling with more useful robot behavior, without treating every ambiguous instruction as requiring another question.
neurips-2024-introspective-planning-alig.tldr: Introspective planning retrieves reasoning examples to improve robot safety and compliance while better matching uncertainty to ambiguous instructions.

paragraphs: Transformers become expensive on long sequences because attention has quadratic complexity, and extending beyond familiar sequence lengths can be difficult. Existing approaches with lower computational growth can sacrifice training efficiency or task accuracy. Megalodon introduces a sequence-modeling architecture designed for unlimited context length while addressing this efficiency and performance tradeoff.

The architecture builds on MEGA, which combines exponential moving averages with gated attention. Megalodon adds complex exponential moving averages, timestep normalization, normalized attention, and a pre-normalization arrangement with two-hop residual connections. These components are introduced to improve the model’s capabilities and training stability as part of a unified architecture.

In a controlled comparison at seven billion parameters and two trillion training tokens, Megalodon achieves better efficiency than the transformer comparison. Its training loss is 1.70, between LLaMA2-7B at 1.75 and LLaMA2-13B at 1.67. The authors also report consistent advantages across evaluated tasks, domains, and modalities. These results support the architecture’s practical promise alongside its long-context design, with the numerical comparison tied to the stated training scale.
neurips-2024-megalodon-efficient-llm-pre.tldr: Megalodon combines moving-average sequence modeling with gated attention and stability improvements to support long contexts with strong reported efficiency and performance.

paragraphs: Object-based visual reasoning needs representations that describe objects richly while keeping their concepts distinct. When those concepts are learned without labels, users also need ways to inspect them and correct mistakes. Neural Concept Binder addresses these needs through structured concept-slot encodings that support both continuous and discrete representations.

The framework uses two stages of binding. Soft binding applies the SysBinder mechanism to obtain encodings of object factors. Hard binding then uses hierarchical clustering and retrieval-based inference to produce discrete representations from unlabeled images. This combination connects expressive learned features with a structured form that can be examined and revised.

The authors show that hard binding preserves model performance while supporting integration with both neural and symbolic reasoning modules. The representation also accommodates external knowledge, including human input and insights from another AI model. Evaluations use the newly introduced CLEVR-Sudoku dataset. The contribution is a way to make unsupervised visual concepts more accessible for inspection and correction while retaining their usefulness in complex reasoning tasks.
neurips-2024-neural-concept-binder-73bbd.tldr: Neural Concept Binder turns unlabeled images into inspectable concept representations that support correction and both neural and symbolic reasoning.

paragraphs: Image segmentation systems can identify detailed regions but typically lack conversational reasoning and text-based control. Large vision-language models offer conversation and reasoning, yet struggle with precise pixel-level understanding and flexible visual prompts. OMG-LLaVA brings these abilities together so a single model can respond to text and visual inputs at several levels of detail.

The framework uses a universal segmentation model as its visual encoder. It converts image information, perception priors, and visual prompts into visual tokens for a language model. A perception prior embedding helps combine those priors with image features. The language model interprets the user’s instructions and supports both textual responses and segmentation outputs.

The resulting system handles reasoning about whole images, individual objects, and pixels within one architecture containing an encoder, a decoder, and a language model. On multiple benchmarks, it matches or exceeds specialized methods. These findings support the feasibility of training a unified system end to end while preserving detailed visual understanding and adding flexible instruction-driven interaction.
neurips-2024-omg-llava-bridging-image-le.tldr: OMG-LLaVA combines segmentation and language reasoning in one model that accepts text and visual prompts and returns text or pixel-level outputs.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a learning scheme for functional differential equations, which arise in physics, mathematics, and optimal control. Its starting problem is a tradeoff: numerical analysis can be prohibitively expensive, while existing approximations often simplify solutions too much. The authors combine a mathematical approximation with physics-informed neural networks to address both concerns.

The mathematical component is cylindrical approximation. It represents functions and functional derivatives using an orthonormal basis, turning the original functional differential equations into high-dimensional partial differential equations. This transformation makes the problem accessible to a different numerical solver, although the resulting equations still require a method capable of handling many dimensions.

The authors prove convergence theorems for the approximated functional derivatives and solutions, providing theoretical support for the transformation. They then use physics-informed neural networks to solve the resulting equations numerically. The abstract reports that this combination handles a broader class of functional derivatives more efficiently than conventional discretization methods, improving the approximation’s scalability.

Experiments on two functional differential equations provide a proof of concept. The reported relative L1 errors are around one thousandth, an order the authors describe as typical for physics-informed neural networks. These results demonstrate numerical success on the two tested equations, while the convergence results provide a mathematical foundation for the approximation underlying the approach.
neurips-2024-physics-informed-neural-net.tldr: The paper combines cylindrical approximation with physics-informed neural networks to solve functional differential equations, proving approximation convergence and demonstrating accuracy on two examples.

paragraphs: Poseidon is a foundation model for learning PDE solution operators, the mappings used to obtain solutions across different problem inputs. The goal is to learn reusable representations during pretraining that help with new equations downstream. The model uses a multiscale operator transformer and time-conditioned normalization layers to support evaluation at continuous times.

Its training strategy uses the semigroup property of time-dependent PDEs, which relates evolution across a time interval to evolution over successive intervals. This provides a way to expand the available training data substantially. Poseidon is pretrained on a large, diverse fluid-dynamics dataset, drawing its initial experience from a small set of governing equations.

Across 15 downstream tasks covering varied PDE types and operators, the authors report substantial improvements over baselines in accuracy and sample efficiency. They also find strong generalization to physics absent from pretraining and favorable scaling with model and data size. These results support the potential for transferable PDE representations, including transfer to unseen and unrelated equations in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2024-poseidon-efficient-foundati.tldr: Poseidon learns transferable PDE representations from fluid-dynamics pretraining, improving accuracy and sample efficiency across diverse downstream equation-solving tasks.

paragraphs: Parametric Piecewise Linear Networks are designed for visual inference involving time. Their motivation comes from biological neural behavior and event cameras, which are built to imitate aspects of retinal activity. The paper explores how an artificial neuron’s internal representation can be designed to suit this kind of temporally changing visual input.

The central choice is to represent a neuron’s membrane potential using a piecewise linear function with learnable coefficients. This allows training to adjust the function that describes the neuron’s potential. The design shares the broader idea of constructing deep models from trainable parametric functions, an idea also associated with Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks.

The authors evaluate PPLNs in event-based and conventional image-based vision applications. They report state-of-the-art performance on tasks including steering prediction, human pose estimation, and motion deblurring. The findings give empirical support to the proposed neuron representation across several visual problems. They also show that the architecture’s usefulness in the reported experiments extends beyond the event-camera setting that motivated its design.
neurips-2024-pplns-parametric-piecewise-.tldr: PPLNs model artificial-neuron potentials with learnable piecewise linear functions and report strong results across event-based and image-based vision tasks.

paragraphs: Small tabular datasets can make classification difficult, especially in fields where collecting observations is costly. Generating synthetic rows could help, but a generator trained on little data may overfit and produce examples that reduce classification accuracy. TabEBM addresses this problem with an approach that models each class separately.

The method builds a distinct energy-based generative model for every class, with each model learning its own class-specific data distribution. This differs from using one shared model to approximate all class-conditional distributions. The authors describe the resulting energy landscapes as robust even when class distributions are ambiguous, making the separation between class-specific generators central to the method.

Experiments report higher-quality synthetic data and better statistical fidelity than existing methods. Adding these generated examples to training data consistently improves classification across the evaluated datasets and sizes, with particular benefits for small datasets. The findings support separate class-specific energy models as a useful way to generate augmentation data when limited observations make shared generative modeling difficult.
neurips-2024-tabebm-a-tabular-data-augme.tldr: TabEBM trains a separate energy-based generator for each class to produce synthetic tabular data that improves classification, especially on small datasets.

paragraphs: Practical stochastic gradient descent often processes examples without replacement, possibly reshuffling them each epoch. Traditional analysis more commonly assumes sampling with replacement. Although shuffled SGD has received theoretical treatment, this paper argues that existing bounds remain too pessimistic to account for the advantages often observed when training with data permutations.

The authors analyze shuffled SGD through its relationship to primal-dual cyclic coordinate methods. They introduce more detailed smoothness parameters to capture structure that earlier bounds miss. Their framework covers smooth and non-smooth convex losses and produces tighter convergence bounds for the shuffling schemes identified as IG, SO, and RR.

The new bounds predict convergence improvements over previous theoretical bounds by up to a factor of O(√n), where n is the dataset size. This is an improvement in the analysis of convergence, rather than a reported implementation speedup. Numerical studies on common machine learning datasets show that the bounds are substantially tighter. The work helps reconcile existing shuffled optimization practice with a more informative theoretical account of its behavior.
neurips-2024-tighter-convergence-bounds-.tldr: A primal-dual analysis yields tighter convergence bounds for shuffled SGD on convex losses, helping explain its observed practical advantages.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary 3D detection aims to recognize new object classes in unfamiliar environments. Systems based on point clouds can be expensive to deploy because they rely on specialized sensing. OVM3D-Det instead trains a detector from RGB images alone, avoiding high-precision LiDAR or other 3D sensor data for both inputs and the creation of training boxes.

The framework combines open-vocabulary 2D models with pseudo-LiDAR to automatically produce 3D object labels from images. Those labels are imperfect: noisy point clouds and heavily occluded objects can yield inaccurate boxes. The authors address this with adaptive pseudo-LiDAR erosion and bounding-box refinement informed by prior knowledge from large language models.

These refinements calibrate the generated labels so they can support RGB-only training of monocular 3D detectors. Experiments report better performance than baselines in both indoor and outdoor settings. The contribution is a training pipeline that makes use of widely available images while explicitly improving the quality of the automatically inferred 3D supervision.
neurips-2024-training-an-open-vocabulary.tldr: OVM3D-Det trains open-vocabulary 3D detectors from RGB images by generating and refining 3D labels without 3D sensor data.

paragraphs: In-context learning changes a model’s behavior through its prompt rather than through additional weight updates. This paper asks whether fully recurrent models can be universal in-context approximators: models capable of approximating arbitrary functions through prompting. Earlier results for transformers depended on attention, leaving the corresponding question for recurrent architectures unresolved.

The authors show that several recurrent families can have this capability, including RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs, linear RNNs, and linear gated architectures such as Mamba and Hawk/Griffin. To organize the constructions, they introduce LSRL, a programming language that compiles into these architectures. This gives a common way to express computations and realize them within different recurrent models.

The study also examines multiplicative gating. Architectures with such gates can implement certain operations more stably, making them more promising candidates for practical universal approximation through context. The result establishes a representational capability of these model families; the stability analysis helps distinguish possible constructions from more practically viable ones. LSRL may additionally support future work such as interpretability benchmark construction.
neurips-2024-universal-in-context-approx.tldr: The paper proves that several fully recurrent architectures can be universal in-context approximators and identifies gating as helpful for stable implementations.
